messages.subject: Introductory distance sampling workshop 3-6 December in Tampa
messages.subject_clean: Introductory distance sampling workshop 3-6 December in Tampa
messages.body_plain:
Places are still available for an introductory distance sampling
workshop to be held at the Tampa Marriott Westshore 3-6 December 2011.
The workshop will immediately follow the conclusion of the Marine Mammal
Conference being held in Tampa and will be presented by Prof. Steve
Buckland and Dr. Len Thomas along with others from the Univ. of St.
Andrews.

Please consult the website
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/floridaoverview.html)
for a description of the workshop content and the registration process.

Registration is a five step process:

1) visit
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/floridaoverview.html
and click on the 'Registration' menu option, there you will find a link
to the 'registration form.'
2) complete the registration form and email or fax it back to Rhona (as
described on the form),
3) follow the link on the Word registration form (page 2) to go to the
St. Andrews on-line shop to make payment,
4) return to the Registration page in your browser and complete the
questionnaire at the bottom of the page to provide us with additional
information about you so we can organise our materials to suit, and finally
5) optionally return to the "Florida overview" web page and near the
bottom of that page you will find a link to the hotel hosting the
workshop where you can make room reservations.

--
Eric Rexstad
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews
St. Andrews Scotland KY16 9LZ
+44 (0)1334 461833

messages.subject_clean: Sensitivity of chi-square GOF test to interval cutpoints
messages.body_plain:
Sharon-

It sounds like your measurements have been rounded but that is only a=20
guess. AIC is useful for selecting a model from competing models and=20
goodness of fit provides a guide to the adequacy of model fit.  I use=20
the term "guide" because as you see, the results can depend on the cut=20
points although not usually that much.  The K-S and Cramer-VonMises test=20
are 2 alternatives if your distances are not collected in intervals, but=20
they can be sensitive to rounding.  You should use the gof tests to=20
identify important problem areas with the model fit/data collection.

--jeff

messages.body_plain:
Sharon, if you rely on chi-sq gof, you need to choose cutpoints well away f=
rom favoured rounding distances. If you do, you shouldn't see that level of=
 sensitivity. Without careful choice of cut-points, gof isn't very useful i=
f you have heaping. It's not telling you about model mis-fit - just that yo=
u have a problem with the data.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: MRDS perpendicular distance
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

Please would clear this up from me.  I have double platform, trial
configuration data for common dolphins, which I'm analysing with MRDS in
Distance 6.  Which perpendicular range should I use for duplicate trials -
Obs1 (primary platform) or Obs2 (tracker platform who set the trials)?  I
understand that I should enter the same distance for both data sheet rows
for the same object.

I began with some CDS exploration of the Obs1 data, looking at truncation,
interval bins, and then model selection.  Then I moved on to the MRDS full
independence fitting method.  My understanding was that as I was using the
Obs1 data in the DS part of the model, I should use the these ranges for
Obs1 sightings including the duplicates.  But, if a mixture of Obs1 ranges
(duplicates) and Obs2 ranges (unsuccessful trials) were used in the MRDS
part of the model, to model the conditional detection function, wouldn't
there be a bias towards ranges closer to the vessel - duplicates would
likely have smaller ranges than unsuccessful Obs2 trials?

Alternatively, how could I use the Obs2 ranges for the duplicates - there
was a reduction in range between the initial (or even last re-sighted)
tracker range and the Obs1 range, so this would skew the distribution of
ranges to the right?  I guess I should use the last re-sighting range rather
than the initial range perhaps.

I'm sure there's a simple answer to this - please excuse my lack of
understanding, I couldn't find the answer in the standard texts or Distance
help.

Thanks,

Chris

messages.subject: Re: MRDS perpendicular distance
messages.body_plain:
On 9/12/2011 8:36 AM, Chris Pierpoint wrote:
> > Dear All,
> >
> >
> >
> > Please would clear this up from me.  I have double platform, trial
> > configuration data for common dolphins, which I'm analysing with MRDS in
> > Distance 6.  Which perpendicular range should I use for duplicate trials -
> > Obs1 (primary platform) or Obs2 (tracker platform who set the trials)?  I
> > understand that I should enter the same distance for both data sheet rows
> > for the same object.

What do you mean by perpendicular range?  Do you mean what do you set
for the transect (half-)width?

> >
> >
> >
> > I began with some CDS exploration of the Obs1 data, looking at truncation,
> > interval bins, and then model selection.  Then I moved on to the MRDS full
> > independence fitting method.  My understanding was that as I was using the
> > Obs1 data in the DS part of the model, I should use the these ranges for
> > Obs1 sightings including the duplicates.  But, if a mixture of Obs1 ranges
> > (duplicates) and Obs2 ranges (unsuccessful trials) were used in the MRDS
> > part of the model, to model the conditional detection function, wouldn't
> > there be a bias towards ranges closer to the vessel - duplicates would
> > likely have smaller ranges than unsuccessful Obs2 trials?

You need to understand that the full independence models currently in
mrds do not fit a detection model based on distance sampling.  They
solely use the conditional detection function which for the trial
configuration would use obs2 data as trials and would estimate the
detection function of obs1 from the missed/seen by obs1.  For the trial
configuration, the full independence model is simply a logistic
regression. It uses the distances from observer 2 for the trials and
they would be used for the range (width if that is what you mean).

> >
> >
> >
> > Alternatively, how could I use the Obs2 ranges for the duplicates - there
> > was a reduction in range between the initial (or even last re-sighted)
> > tracker range and the Obs1 range, so this would skew the distribution of
> > ranges to the right?  I guess I should use the last re-sighting range rather
> > than the initial range perhaps.

Presumably this is why you are using trial full independence because the
dolphins are being attracted to the boat.  You should use the distance
of the initial sighting by observer 2.  It is for these kind of
circumstances that the trial full independence model is useful.  As you
noted the distances are smaller for observer 1 who is seeing them
sometimes after they have been attracted to the vessel, which is why
those distances are not used in the estimation of obs1 detection
function.  See Buckland S.T., Turnock B.J. (1992) A robust line transect
method. Biometrics 48:901-909

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Grouped Point Transects and estimating variance
messages.subject_clean: Grouped Point Transects and estimating variance
messages.body_plain:
Sorry if this has been addressed earlier by I could not find anything in
the archives.

If the spatial layout of point transects is such that they are grouped
(e.g., 6 points per group - where the distance among points in each
group is << than the distance among groups) then one might want to
estimate the variance using a bootstrap where the groups are selected
instead of individual points (see pp. 163-164 in Intro book).

My question is how to implement this in DISTANCE. I could see combining
data from each group and setting survey effort to 6 as one approach. But
doesn't this ignore some information about variability among points? It
seems to me it would be preferable to retain the information from
individual points but be able to select them by group in the bootstrap.

Maybe the solution is blindingly obvious... but I can't see it.  Can
this be set up in DISTANCE or do I need to "trick" DISTANCE, such as by
creating strata that indicate the grouping and resample on strata?

Thanks,

Duane

--

messages.subject_clean: Grouped Point Transects and estimating variance
messages.body_plain:
Duane, I would do exactly as you suggest - combine the data from the 6 poin=
ts.  It is the clusters that are the independent sampling units, so assessi=
ng precision on the basis of variation among clusters is correct.

Of course, you could fit a spatial model to your count data, and then you c=
an retain the information from each individual point.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: DSM Prediction grid
messages.body_plain:
Gareth:

If your study area is large, the portion of the study area around the
perimeter that does not fall into the prediction grid cell squares will
be small; and the approximation for the purposes of estimating abundance
will be adequate.

We have not worked with prediction grid cells that (by and large) are
not square.  I suppose you could use some sort of tessellation but that
will make it more difficult to organise your covariate values.  As a
rule the covariate data we have used for DSM analyses come to use from
remotely sensed data that are squares.  All said and done, your life
will be simplest if you use your first option.

On to your next question:  'can I speed variance estimation
calculations' the simple answer is no.  Bootstrap calculations are by
definition computationally expensive.  You'll not speed the calculations
appreciably by moving your analysis directly into R.  Your strategy of
making your segments as small as possible will cost you computing time,
as you have found.  You might consider increasing your segment lengths
to bring down your computing burden.  Model results tend to be (fairly)
robust to choice of segment size.  Consider the scale of the covariates
you wish to use when debating the size of your segments.

messages.subject: Combining aerial photography and MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

We conducted an aerial survey for narwhals using a double-observer distan=
ce sampling protocol. Concurrently, using two cameras angled obliquely, w=
e took aerial photos of the area directly below the plane and out to eith=
er side. Approximately a third of the area covered by the photographs was=
 also visible to the observers.=20

The plan is to conduct MRDS analysis in Distance to calculate the abundan=
ce of the population. Unfortunately, two of our observers, one on either =
side, appear to have missed many observations or not measured declination=
 angles. Specifically, they did not site many animals missed by the other=
 two more-experienced observers. I consequently suspect that we will not =
have a sufficient correction of =E2=80=9Cperception bias=E2=80=9D (animal=
s visible but not observed). We know from previous surveys that our obser=
vers are missing animals at the trackline and would like to correct this =
negative bias. To be clear, we know that animals are being missed within =
the region visible to the observers at the bubble windows, not only direc=
tly below the plane.=20

I=E2=80=99m wondering if there is a way to use the aerial photographs to =
correct for missed animals. Unfortunately, we have approximately 40,000 p=
hotos and no time to view them all. Our sightings are quite patchy, with =
many transects having 0 sightings. I=E2=80=99m wondering if anyone has a =
suggestion for an effective way to sub-sample the photos to establish a c=
orrection factor for the visual observations. Specifically, could we focu=
s our efforts on transects with sightings? The narwhal density is likely =
low enough that randomly sub-sampling the photos may not lead to many sig=
htings.=20

Any advice would be greatly appreciated. Feel free to respond directly to=
 me and I=E2=80=99ll collate the responses and post them back to the list=
.=20

Sincerely, Natalie.=20=20

messages.subject: Re: Changing data column from text to decimal
messages.subject_clean: Changing data column from text to decimal
messages.body_plain:
Sorry Philip, there's no labour saving way to do this I'm afraid.  I suggest you
delete the offending columns, then add them again as decimal, then re-import
your data.  The whole process will hopefully only take a few minutes (depending
on how much data you have, as the import can be slow for very big datasets).

Why can't it change the type? This is because the distance data file is actually
a database (Microsoft Access format), and you can't change the type of a field
in a database.  I could have written code that gets around this by allowing you
to choose a new type, then add a temporary field of the new type, convert and
copy the data, delete the old field, rename the new field (you can rename).
However, I was worried that the type conversion would not go smoothly, and it
seemed such an obscure feature I didn't get around to it.  If you think it would
be useful then please go to the Distance web site, click on "report a bug" and
use the Bugzilla site to request it as a feature.

Cheers - Len

--

messages.subject: Dealing with track avoidence
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been sampling kangaroo density along tracks, and have
used animals with GPS collars to test whether tracks are being avoided. The results
suggest kangaroos tend to be between 6-11% further form track than expected, had
distribution been completely random. This difference was significant within 50m
and 100m from track, but not at 200m.

Avoidance is not a strict non use of area near track, rather
a tendency to be further away, which makes it difficult to deal with. How
exactly can this type of avoidance me dealt with?

The only idea I had was to model the affect of avoidance as distance
from line increases, and adjust kangaroo distance (from sampling) values
accordingly. For example, kangaroos tend to be 9% further from line at 50m, 11%
at 100m and 6% at 200m, so adjustment term could be created. This approach does
not allow me to take into account tracks over the entire study region however.

The only approach I have seen applied, is to left truncate
to the point of avoidance, then remove that area of avoidance from the study
region. This is not possible here, as there is no strict no use area.

A quick side issue. I have seen left truncation applied to dealing
with reactive movement and track avoidance. My understanding is left truncation
is not justified in dealing with reactive movement. Am I right is this thought?

And yes I agree sampling along tracks is not a good idea for
numerous reasons, including the occurrence of track avoidance :)

Cheers

Brett

--
Brett Howland
PhD Candidate
Fenner School of Environment and Society
ANU College of Medicine, Biology & Environment
The Australian National University

messages.subject: Re: Dealing with track avoidence
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brett,

I would say that if you know the "true" distribution of animals with respect to
distance from the transect line from your radio data, then you can combine this
knowledge with observed distances to estimate the detection function.  This
approach is detailed in Tiago Marques' PhD thesis, which is available at
http://hdl.handle.net/10023/391
see chapters 4 and 5.  You can't do it in Distance, but the methods could be
programmed in R.

Regarding left truncation, it seems OK if the animals within some distance x
tend to show responsive movement and leave the area completely (so they are not
counted at all within the right truncation w).  But it's not OK if they leave
the strip out to distance x but move out a bit into distances between x and w.
Then left truncation will produce a positive bias in the density estimate.

Good luck!

  - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: Changing data column from text to decimal
messages.subject_clean: Changing data column from text to decimal
messages.body_plain:
> > 1. Can't you go into the

> > DistData mdb and change the field type without needing to re-import
> > everything? My very large dataset is a drag to keep re-importing.

Yes, you can do this, if you have an ancient version of Access, or your version
will allow you to upgrade the database but then export it afterwards back into
Microsoft Access 2.0 format.  The "native" version of Access to use is Access
97.  Note that it is not sufficient to change the field type; you also have to
change the entry in the DataFields table corresponding with that field -- change
the FieldType from 3 (i.e., Text) to either 2 (Decimal) or 1 (Integer).  The
format of the DistaData.mdb is documented in a help appendix "Inside Distance".

I didn't mention this before as it's black-belt stuff.  But you're clearly a ninja.

> > 2. Why is
> > the DistData mdb created in an ancient version of Microsoft Access that makes
> > it impossible to edit using queries and such if you only have Access 2007 or
> > newer? Is it so that clumsy tinkerers like me don't screw it up?

Not at all.  It's because Distance is ancient!  When I wrote the database
interface, this stuff was cutting edge!  Since then Microsoft have completely
changed the way you can program database stuff twice -- this is not something we
have the resources to keep up with I'm afraid.

Cheers - Len
